record.label: France—overlapping administrative, judicial, and ecclesiastical divisions
record.meaning: Provinces, generalities, intendancies, parlementary ressorts, archiepiscopal provinces, and dioceses overlapped and generated recurrent jurisdictional conflict. Provinces, generalities, parlementary ressorts, dioceses, and local jurisdictions overlapped because the Crown accumulated and adapted inherited institutions rather than imposing uniform structures. Ancient, unequal provinces and largely honorary governors coexisted with newer, more uniform generalities administered by intendants. The Church divided France into archiepiscopal provinces and dioceses whose boundaries and jurisdictional enclaves followed another nonuniform geography.
record.stance: The pattern was uneven and illogical in appearance, yet historically rooted and central to how the kingdom functioned. Treat fragmentation as historically rooted and partly functional, not merely irrational disorder. Preserve the distinction between provincial identity and operative royal administration. Treat ecclesiastical geography as an additional layer of jurisdictional pluralism.
acceptable_access: France—overlapping administrative, judicial, and ecclesiastical divisions

record.label: Administrative reorganization into departments, districts, and communes
record.meaning: The Assembly replaced historically varied provinces and intendancies with eighty-three departments, districts and elected communes, despite mandates defending particular privileges. This uniform but decentralized elected structure also displaced the improvised authorities of July 1789 in 1790. Fear of anarchy and new opportunities for office drew lawyers, businesspeople, merchants, tradesmen, artisans, and other property holders into political administration. Historic liberties and exemptions of provinces, towns, corporations, and judicial bodies were renounced, clearing the way for uniform national institutions. The Assembly replaced France's diverse provinces and jurisdictions with eighty-three departments subdivided into districts and communes governed by elected bodies. The new state combined uniform territorial structures with near-total dependence on locally elected, often unpaid and inexperienced officials. The 1790 local elections replaced the varied committees and arrangements of July 1789 with standardized mayors, procurators, councils, and urban sections. The eligible caption identifies departments of revolutionary France; it adds no geographical access requirement. Weak local enforcement limited administration more broadly than tax collection alone.
record.stance: Broad property-owning participation and shifting recruitment did not mean universal participation. Officials were often unpaid, and goodwill coexisted with weak administrative capacity. The eligible departmental caption identifies the topic only; geographical boundaries and locations inside the map are excluded. The author depicts broad but socially bounded participation: property owners rally to stabilize revolution, and later hundreds of thousands embrace public roles. The author stresses that many deputies lacked electoral mandates for this destruction of local diversity. The reform embodies both national uniformity and radical decentralization, eliminating old territorial privilege while refusing central appointment. The author treats decentralization as an anti-despotic principle whose practical effect was uneven capacity to implement an unprecedented legislative program. The elections mark both a break with the old regime and a second institutional break with the improvised municipal revolution. Caption topic only; map boundaries, cities and annexations are excluded.

record.label: Paris sections and Cordeliers organization
record.meaning: Replacing Paris’s sixty districts with forty-eight sections was intended to weaken local radicalism, but Danton’s organization survived. A press-backed local political machine could sustain influence and national ambition despite institutional reorganization. The redivision of Paris into forty-eight electoral sections was intended to weaken radical districts but instead provided enduring bases for popular intervention. Danton's local political machine linked district organization and radical newspapers and successfully transferred its influence into the new sectional system.
record.stance: Preserve intended containment and actual organizational continuity. The eligible Paris caption identifies sections and main places and streets only; locations, numbered keys and other map interiors impose no access requirement. The legislators' attempt at control is portrayed as unsuccessful because activists adapted the new structure to continued national influence. The author emphasizes Danton's ambition, opportunism, and organizational ingenuity rather than treating section radicalism as spontaneous alone.
acceptable_access: Danton, the Cordeliers district, and the Théâtre-Français section
